title: == or equals?
intro: `a == b` asks whether two variables point at the same array. `Arrays.equals(a, b)` compares what's inside, box by box. Judge both, for four different pairs.

rightEach.==: Both arrows end at the same array, so `a == b` is `true`.

rounds.right: `b = a` gives one array a second name: `==` is `true`, and so is `Arrays.equals`.

why.==: `int[] b = a;` copies the arrow, not the array: both variables point at the very same array, and `==` compares the arrows.
why.equals: There is only one array here, and an array always matches itself, box for box.

rightEach.==: Two arrows, two different arrays: `a == b` is `false`.

rounds.right: A clone is a different array with the same contents: `==` says `false`, `Arrays.equals` says `true`.

why.==: `clone()` builds a brand-new array with boxes of its own, so `a` and `b` point at two different objects.
why.equals: The clone holds the same values in the same order, and that is all `Arrays.equals` looks at.

rightEach.==: Two arrows, two different arrays: `a == b` is `false`.

rounds.right: Two arrays that happen to hold the same values: different objects, equal contents.

why.==: Each `{…}` literal builds an array of its own, so `a` and `b` point at two different arrays, even though their values match.
why.equals: Same length, same values, in the same order: compared box by box, everything matches.

rightEach.==: Two arrows, two different arrays: `a == b` is `false`.

rounds.right: Different arrays with different contents: both are `false`. Order counts too, because `Arrays.equals` compares box 0 with box 0, box 1 with box 1, and so on.

why.==: Two separate literals make two separate arrays: `==` compares the arrows, and they end in different places.
why.equals: `Arrays.equals` compares box by box, and box {diff} differs: {av} in `a`, {bv} in `b`.
